messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Combat Pilot
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 46

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rangi Tūhoe is a 54-year-old Māori man, married and currently serving as a combat pilot with decades of operational experience behind him. He was referred for psychological assessment following a life-threatening accident that occurred eight months ago during a routine training sortie, and he has only recently agreed to engage with mental health support — a decision that, by his own account, took considerable internal negotiation.

The incident occurred when a catastrophic mechanical failure caused Rangi's aircraft to enter an uncontrolled descent at low altitude. For approximately forty seconds — a duration he can reconstruct with meticulous, almost clinical precision — he worked through emergency procedures while the aircraft continued to fall. He ejected at the last viable moment, sustaining significant physical injuries on landing in rough terrain. What he describes most vividly, however, is not the physical impact but the forty seconds themselves: the particular quality of the cockpit sounds as warning systems cascaded, the sensation of the stick offering nothing, the moment he understood that the aircraft would not recover. He survived. The aircraft did not.

In the weeks that followed, once his physical injuries had stabilised, Rangi noticed that something in him had not returned to baseline alongside his body. He continued to report for duty in a limited capacity, and it was here — in the very environment that had defined his professional identity for thirty years — that the first persistent difficulties announced themselves. Warning tones during simulator sessions, the particular vibration signature of certain aircraft on the flight line, and the visual geometry of low-altitude approaches had each become charged with a quality he struggled to articulate. He would feel his attention narrow and his body organise itself around the possibility of emergency, even in conditions that were objectively controlled and safe.

What Rangi had not anticipated was how far this watchfulness would travel beyond the cockpit. At home, in the house he shares with his wife Aroha, he found himself unable to sit with his back to a doorway, unable to settle into a room without first noting the exits. He would stand briefly at the threshold of their kitchen or living room, eyes moving to windows and doors before he allowed himself to enter fully. Aroha noticed before he named it. He told her it was habit, a pilot's situational awareness. He had come to believe, in a way that felt entirely rational to him, that this monitoring was simply what a man in his position owed to himself and his family — that to stop scanning would be to make the same mistake twice.

Alongside the hypervigilance, something quieter and more frightening had taken hold. Rangi found himself sitting across from Aroha at dinner, watching her laugh at something on television, and feeling a distance he could not bridge — not anger, not sadness exactly, but an absence where feeling should have been. He had come to believe that whatever the accident had taken from him in those forty seconds, it had taken something irreversible. He no longer recognised himself in his own responses. The man who had once felt fierce pride at his daughter's graduation, who had wept privately when his father died, seemed to have belonged to a version of himself that no longer existed. He was certain the damage was permanent — not a wound in recovery, but a structural change, the way metal fatigues and does not return to its original form.

This conviction had shaped the months since the accident in ways that had quietly accumulated. He had declined invitations from colleagues, shortened conversations with Aroha, and stopped attending the community gatherings that had anchored his sense of belonging within his whānau. Aroha had eventually told him plainly that she was losing him, not to absence but to a version of him she did not know. It was this — not the sleeplessness, not the vigilance, not the clinical recommendation — that finally brought him to seek help.

What Rangi fears most is confirmation of what he already suspects: that the person he was before the descent is gone, and that no amount of talking will retrieve him. What he hopes for, more quietly, is to be wrong.
